strengths: The manuscript is clearly organized and gives a reasonably concrete description of OVSegDT, including its architecture, objectives, entropy gate, and principal hyperparameters. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/87927703498c4ceb8a00050d251e818d/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The practical goal is worthwhile: improving open-vocabulary navigation without depth, odometry, explicit mapping, or a large policy model would be useful for embodied vision.

On HM3D-OVON val-unseen, the deployable YOLOE-based system obtains competitive performance (40.1% SR and 20.9% SPL), and the ground-truth-mask experiment shows that reliable target localization could provide a large gain over the DagRL baseline.

The component studies separately examine entropy-adaptive training, mask input, auxiliary segmentation, mask filtering, and detector calibration. Reporting three-run means and deviations, collisions, training curves, and statistical tests is more informative than reporting SR alone.

The predicted-mask results expose the substantial gap between oracle segmentation (70.4% SR) and realistic YOLOE segmentation (40.1% SR), rather than hiding the method's dependence on perception quality.
weaknesses: The principal 40.1% SR result is not supported by a clearly leakage-free calibration protocol. The paper tunes category-specific YOLOE confidence thresholds, analyzes the optimal thresholds on the val-seen, val-seen-synonyms, and val-unseen splits, and then reports the calibrated model on val-unseen. It specifies neither a disjoint calibration split nor a rule chosen without validation outcomes. Consequently, the central open-vocabulary result may incorporate evaluation-set tuning and cannot be interpreted reliably as generalization to unseen categories.

Several headline claims are overstated. OVSegDT does not achieve the highest val-unseen SR in Table 1 (MTU3D reports 40.8 versus 40.1), and its advantage over Uni-NaVid is only 0.6 SR and 1.1 SPL without a controlled significance comparison. The claimed 33% sample-complexity reduction largely compares a 200M-step run with DagRL's 300M-step run; no matched-performance sample-efficiency analysis across seeds establishes that percentage.

The evidence for the auxiliary segmentation contribution is weak and mixed. The decoder reconstructs the same target mask already supplied to the policy, making the objective close to mask autoencoding rather than an independently supervised semantic task. It raises oracle-mask SR only from 69.3 to 70.4 while reducing SPL from 40.8 to 39.4 and increasing collisions from 14.5 to 18.8. Thus, the claimed improvement in navigation quality is not supported across the reported metrics.

EALM is described as a per-sample scheduler, but the method computes entropy per mini-batch and applies one EMA-derived coefficient to the combined losses. The paper does not ablate the entropy bounds or EMA factor, compare against tuned continuous schedules, or explain whether BC and PPO batches have compatible sampling and loss scales. These omissions make it difficult to attribute the improvement specifically to entropy adaptation.

Calling collision count a safety metric is insufficiently justified. Collision count is confounded by episode length, success, and how much the agent moves—the nearly inactive PPO baseline has the fewest collisions while essentially never succeeding. Collision rate per traveled distance or action, success-conditioned collisions, and explicit safety evaluation would be needed to support the safety claims.

Evaluation is confined to one simulator benchmark and category-name goals. There is no cross-dataset, real-robot, detector-shift, or systematic mask-corruption evaluation. This is especially limiting because the introduction frames arbitrary free-form goals and real-world deployment, while the conclusion concedes that the system cannot follow free-form instructions.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: the paper does not provide the full category-specific calibration thresholds or selection procedure, exact episode counts, detailed DAgger/PPO data-collection mechanics, or usable source code despite referring to a code appendix; the title-page code link is blank. The n=3 one-sided unpaired t-tests also provide fragile statistical evidence and do not address the main comparisons in Table 1.

Overall, the method has useful empirical ideas and promising results, but uncertainty about validation-set calibration directly affects the primary reported result, while the novelty and evidence for EALM and the auxiliary loss are not yet strong enough to offset that concern. These are material scientific issues rather than presentation refinements.

strengths: OVSegDT addresses an important embodied-vision problem and achieves strong HM3D-OVON val-unseen results (40.1% SR and 20.9% SPL) without depth or odometry.
The ablations demonstrate that target masks are highly useful: with ground-truth masks, val-unseen SR increases from 20.2% to 69.3%, while collisions decrease from 41.8 to 14.5.

The paper evaluates several imitation/RL schedules and reports three-seed variation, collision counts, training curves, and component ablations. EALM modestly improves over DagRL while using 200M rather than 300M training steps.
The architecture is comparatively lightweight and the manuscript clearly explains its principal components and limitations.
weaknesses: The claimed open-vocabulary generalization is compromised by category-specific YOLOE confidence calibration and vocabulary pruning. The paper analyzes thresholds on the benchmark validation categories, including unseen categories, but does not identify a separate calibration set or protocol. This risks validation-set adaptation and is inconsistent with unrestricted free-form goals; the conclusion itself acknowledges that free-form instructions are unsupported.

The comparison does not cleanly isolate the navigation contribution. OVSegDT receives masks from a strong external open-vocabulary segmenter, while key RGB-only baselines do not. The stated 130M-parameter, low-cost characterization apparently excludes YOLOE, and no total latency, parameter count, or compute including mask generation is reported. Against the more comparable detector-based DAgRL+OD, the val-unseen gain is only 3.0 SR and 1.1 SPL.

The component ablation is incomplete under the actual predicted-mask setting: there is no mask-conditioned baseline trained without EALM, and the segmentation-loss comparison uses only ground-truth masks. Thus the individual contributions of EALM, mask conditioning, and the auxiliary objective to the final 40.1/20.9 result cannot be determined.

The auxiliary segmentation loss reconstructs a mask that is already supplied as input, is closely related to established auxiliary segmentation objectives, and provides only +1.1 SR with ground-truth masks while degrading SPL from 40.8 to 39.4 and increasing collisions from 14.5 to 18.8. The evidence therefore does not support the claimed broad improvement in navigation quality.

Several claims overstate the tables. OVSegDT does not have the highest val-unseen SR because MTU3D reports 40.8 versus 40.1. EALM also does not yield the lowest collision count among Table 2 methods. Collision count is not a reliable standalone safety measure because it is confounded by episode length and failure behavior, as illustrated by PPO obtaining only 1.3 val-unseen collisions while almost never succeeding.

EALM is described as a per-sample scheduler, but the method computes minibatch entropy and an EMA to produce a shared mixing coefficient. Entropy is not necessarily calibrated uncertainty, and the fixed bounds 0.35 and 0.75 receive no sensitivity analysis. Consequently, the claimed principled and domain-robust transition is insufficiently supported.

Evaluation is confined to one simulator benchmark, with no cross-dataset, real-robot, or detector-shift evaluation. This is especially limiting because the method depends strongly on segmentation: SR falls from 70.4 with ground-truth masks to 35.5 with uncalibrated YOLOE masks.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite the checklist assertions. The manuscript does not provide the complete reward specification, per-category calibration thresholds, detector fine-tuning recipe, evaluation episode counts, or actual source code claimed to appear in a code appendix. The three-run one-sided unpaired t-tests are also fragile, lack multiple-comparison correction, and are poorly matched to paired evaluation on common episodes.

Overall, the empirical results are worthwhile, but benchmark-specific detector calibration, unfair or incomplete controls, modest originality, and multiple unsupported claims currently outweigh the contribution. These are material scientific issues rather than presentation-only refinements.

strengths: The paper addresses an important embodied-vision problem and presents a practical RGB-only pipeline combining a compact transformer policy, open-vocabulary segmentation cues, and joint imitation/RL training.

The reported HM3D-OVON results are strong: OVSegDT achieves 40.1% SR and 20.9% SPL on val-unseen, with similar performance on seen and unseen categories. Its val-unseen SPL is the best value in Table 1 despite not using depth or odometry.

The ablations identify a particularly large benefit from the goal mask: with ground-truth masks, val-unseen SR rises from 20.2% to 69.3% and SPL from 8.8% to 40.8%. The predicted-mask experiments also transparently expose the substantial gap between oracle and realistic segmentation.

EALM is simple and potentially useful. At 200M steps it improves over the 300M-step DAgRL result in Table 2 while reducing collisions, and comparisons against PPO, DAgger, a fixed combined loss, and a manually scheduled switch provide meaningful supporting evidence.

The manuscript is generally clear, includes training curves, component ablations, three-run variation for principal results, computational details, and an explicit discussion of dependence on segmentation quality.
weaknesses: The headline val-unseen result appears to use category-specific YOLOE thresholds calibrated by examining navigation success for categories from the same val-unseen split. No independent calibration split is described. This creates evaluation leakage and weakens both the 40.1% SR result and the claim of generalization to unseen categories. The uncalibrated/filtered system obtains only 35.1% SR and 18.5% SPL.

Several claims overstate the evidence. EALM does not achieve the lowest val-unseen collision count in Table 2: its 41.8 collisions are worse than EarlySwitcher at 27.7 and Dagger+PPO at 35.8. Collision count is also not normalized by episode length, so it is an ambiguous safety measure; the failing PPO agent trivially records only 1.3 collisions. Likewise, the stated 33% sample-complexity reduction is inferred from 200M versus 300M training budgets rather than from matched learning curves on validation performance, and the appendix separately claims a twofold speedup.

EALM is described as per-sample modulation, but the equations define a single coefficient from an exponential moving average of mini-batch entropy. Thus it is batch/global scheduling, not per-sample adaptation. Its originality is modest, and there is no sensitivity analysis for the manually selected entropy bounds or comparison with equivalently tuned smooth schedules. The mechanism can also treat an incorrectly confident policy as ready for PPO.

The auxiliary segmentation objective provides mixed evidence: with oracle masks it increases SR only from 69.3% to 70.4% while decreasing SPL from 40.8% to 39.4% and increasing collisions from 14.5 to 18.8. Because the target mask is already an input, reconstructing it may amount to an easy autoencoding objective; the experiments do not substantiate the claimed disentanglement or show its benefit with predicted masks.

Evaluation is confined to one simulator benchmark, with no cross-dataset or physical-robot test. Comparisons in Table 1 combine numbers from systems with substantially different components, and the claim of overall state of the art is imprecise because MTU3D reports higher val-unseen SR, although OVSegDT has higher SPL and fewer sensor requirements.

Reproducibility is presently incomplete: the code link is blank, category-specific detector thresholds are not enumerated, and important details of joint DAgger/PPO data construction, reward coefficients, segmentation-loss weighting, detector preprocessing, and software versions are absent. Statistical conclusions based on one-sided unpaired t-tests over only three seeds should also be interpreted cautiously.

The task is repeatedly framed as accepting free-form language, but the experiments use category names and the conclusion acknowledges that the method cannot follow free-form instructions. Moreover, Table 11 shows near-total failure when the externally generated mask is removed, indicating that open-vocabulary recognition is primarily delegated to YOLOE rather than learned by the navigation policy.

strengths: The paper addresses an important embodied-vision problem and presents a coherent lightweight system combining mask-conditioned navigation, entropy-adaptive imitation/RL training, and adaptation to predicted open-vocabulary segmentation.

The reported HM3D-OVON performance is strong: OVSegDT reaches 44.7% SR and 20.6% SPL on val-unseen without depth or odometry, outperforming the listed RGB-only methods and remaining competitive with more sensor-heavy systems.

The empirical analysis is broader than a single headline comparison. It includes switching-strategy comparisons, component ablations, predicted-versus-ground-truth masks, failure categories, segmentation error analysis, three-seed results, latency measurements, and limited robot demonstrations.

The paper explicitly studies the realistic degradation caused by predicted segmentation: performance falls from 69.3% SR with ground-truth masks to 28.8% with uncalibrated YOLOE, and the failure analysis identifies recognition as the dominant error source.

The manuscript is generally clear, with an understandable architecture and training objective, informative figures, and candid acknowledgment that the method depends heavily on segmentation quality and exhibits risky near-goal behavior.
weaknesses: The headline val-unseen result is not a clean held-out evaluation. OVSegDT uses category-specific YOLOE confidence calibration, while Supplementary Fig. I explicitly analyzes thresholds according to navigation success on categories from the same val-unseen split, including unseen examples such as plant and mirror. No separate calibration set or threshold-selection protocol is reported. Since calibration raises SR from 28.8% to 35.6% and is required before the fine-tuning result of 44.7%, this apparent validation-split tuning materially undermines the central state-of-the-art and unseen-generalization claims.

The ablations do not fully isolate the claimed architectural contribution. Table 3 lacks an EALM model with a goal mask but without the semantic reward and auxiliary segmentation loss. Consequently, the effect of merely conditioning the policy on the mask cannot be separated from the proposed training objectives, despite claims that the mask encoder itself produces the generalization gain.

The policy's open-vocabulary ability is substantially outsourced to YOLOE and manual vocabulary/threshold processing. Table G shows that the trained policy nearly collapses when given only the text goal (0.1% SR), while mask-only performance is also only 12.6% SR. Thus the evidence supports a tightly coupled text-plus-detector system, not strong language-grounded generalization by the navigation transformer itself.

EALM is a plausible but relatively simple heuristic whose description overstates its granularity and generality. It is called a per-sample scheduler, yet Eq. 5 computes minibatch entropy and applies a globally smoothed EMA gate. Only three nearby values of the lower threshold are tested; the upper threshold, EMA coefficient, action-space transfer rule, and robustness across tasks are not validated. It is also unspecified whether gradients pass through the entropy-derived mixing coefficient.

The safety interpretation is insufficiently supported. Raw collisions are heavily confounded by episode duration, as the authors themselves demonstrate with PPO, and the final full model still averages 45.4 collisions versus 50.2 for DagRL. No normalized collision rate or standard safety metric is reported, and the real-robot section explicitly observes risky behavior near targets. Claims that collision count establishes genuine understanding or safe navigation are therefore too strong.

Reproducibility remains limited: the displayed code link is empty; exact per-category calibration thresholds and their selection data are absent; several DAgger/data-collection and reward details are deferred or underspecified; and the statistical analysis uses one-sided unpaired t-tests with only three seeds, omits tests against the principal state-of-the-art competitors, and reports no multiple-comparison control. The real-world evidence is also only two qualitative demonstrations after retraining for a different camera field of view.

strengths: The paper addresses an important embodied-vision problem and proposes a comparatively lightweight 130M-parameter policy using RGB observations. On HM3D-OVON val-unseen, the complete system reports strong results (44.7% SR and 20.6% SPL), exceeding the listed RGB-only baselines and several systems using additional sensors.

EALM is a simple and potentially useful idea: policy entropy controls the interpolation between behavior cloning and PPO. The comparison against PPO, DAgger, a fixed combined objective, EarlySwitcher, and DagRL provides more evidence than a single-baseline comparison, and EALM reaches competitive performance in 200M rather than 300M reported steps for DagRL.

The authors examine the substantial gap between ground-truth and predicted masks rather than reporting only an oracle setting. The ablations, failure taxonomy, segmentation-error analysis, photometric perturbation test, and onboard latency measurements are useful diagnostic additions.
The manuscript is generally understandable, and it candidly reports that predicted-mask fine-tuning increases collisions and that the real robot exhibits risky behavior near targets.
weaknesses: The central 44.7% val-unseen result appears to depend on category-specific YOLOE threshold calibration selected through navigation success on the evaluation splits. Figures G-I explicitly plot success against thresholds for val seen, synonyms, and unseen categories, but no separate calibration set or selection protocol is identified. Tuning thresholds for val-unseen categories on their evaluation episodes leaks task-specific information, compromises the state-of-the-art comparison, and weakens the claimed open-vocabulary generalization. It also requires advance knowledge and calibration of the deployment vocabulary.

Several headline descriptions do not match the actual method. The system is called end-to-end although it relies on an external open-vocabulary segmentation pipeline and manually calibrated category thresholds. The abstract invokes free-form language, whereas the benchmark supplies category names and the conclusion acknowledges that the method cannot follow free-form instructions. Likewise, EALM is called a per-sample scheduler, but Equations 5-7 describe a mini-batch entropy followed by a global EMA and scalar mixture weight.

The safety claims are not adequately supported. Raw collisions per episode are confounded by episode duration and success, as the paper itself notes for PPO, yet they are still used to claim safer behavior and generalization. No consistently normalized collision rate or success-conditioned comparison is reported for all methods. The final model has 45.4 collisions per episode, more than the 41.8 of the mask-free EALM variant, and the real-robot section reports risky behavior near goals.

The component ablation does not cleanly identify the proposed contributions. Table 3 lacks a goal-mask-only model without the semantic reward and auxiliary loss, and it does not clearly specify which variants receive threshold calibration and predicted-mask fine-tuning. Consequently, the independent contributions of the mask encoder, segmentation objective, reward, calibration, and fine-tuning cannot be determined from the reported rows.

The auxiliary segmentation objective is insufficiently motivated technically. During initial training, the ground-truth mask is already part of the current input, so reconstructing that same mask can amount to a largely trivial autoencoding task. The paper does not show that the objective improves temporal or semantic representations rather than merely copying the input, nor does it compare against simpler mask reconstruction or representation regularizers.

The evidence for EALM's generality and sample-efficiency claims is limited. Only one benchmark and action space are tested; three nearby values of one entropy bound are explored while the other bound and EMA coefficient remain fixed. Reporting a 33% sample-complexity reduction from 200M versus DagRL's 300M-step budget is not a controlled time-to-performance analysis. The asserted mapping from entropy thresholds to top-action probabilities is also not unique without assumptions about the remaining action probabilities.

The statistical analysis is weak: only three runs are used with one-sided unpaired t-tests, no correction is made for multiple comparisons, several ablation entries omit standard deviations, and the unit underlying the tests is not made fully clear. For example, the reported summary statistics do not transparently support all of the very small p-values.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the appendix. Important details include the complete reward coefficients, EALM initialization and entropy aggregation, DAgger/PPO data construction, segmentation-head architecture, category vocabulary and exact threshold list, calibration data-selection protocol, and episode counts. The displayed code-availability statement also contains no usable repository link. The real-world evidence consists of two qualitative demonstrations with a retrained camera-FOV variant and no quantitative success or safety evaluation.

strengths: OVSegDT delivers strong empirical results on HM3D-OVON using only RGB sensing: 44.7% SR and 20.6% SPL on val-unseen, improving substantially over the directly related DagRL baseline and matching or exceeding several methods that use depth, odometry, or much larger vision-language models.

The paper addresses a useful and practically relevant problem: improving open-vocabulary ObjectNav without explicit mapping or expensive language-model planning. Conditioning the policy on an externally predicted target mask is simple, computationally plausible, and demonstrably effective.

The experimental analysis is unusually thorough. Tables 2–5 separately examine optimization strategy, goal-mask conditioning, semantic reward, auxiliary segmentation, detector calibration, predicted-mask fine-tuning, collisions, and failure types. The reported three-seed variation and supplementary significance tests add useful evidence.

EALM is a sensible training mechanism that removes a manually chosen DAgger-to-PPO transition. Under a common architecture and 200M-step budget, it improves val-unseen SR from 14.3–16.4% for alternative switching strategies to 20.2%, while the training curves support smoother and faster convergence.

The paper does not hide the substantial gap between ground-truth and predicted masks: SR falls from 69.3% to 28.8% with unadapted YOLOE. It then quantifies how calibration and predicted-mask fine-tuning recover performance, making the practical contribution more credible.

The presentation is generally clear, and the supplementary material supplies architecture and PPO hyperparameters, entropy-threshold sensitivity, observation ablations, segmentation error analysis, runtime measurements, and illustrative real-robot demonstrations.
weaknesses: The protocol for category-specific YOLOE confidence calibration is a material concern. Figures G–I explicitly analyze success as a function of thresholds on val-seen, val-seen-synonyms, and val-unseen categories, but the manuscript does not state that thresholds were selected without using the evaluated validation episodes. If val-unseen navigation results informed per-category thresholds, the principal unseen-category result is no longer a clean held-out evaluation. Since calibration accounts for a sizable gain from 28.8% to 35.6% SR, this ambiguity affects the central claim.

EALM is described as a “per-sample scheduler,” but Equations 5–7 define entropy over a mini-batch, maintain one exponential moving average, and produce a single mixing coefficient. The manuscript also does not state whether gradients are stopped through the entropy-derived coefficient. Thus, the method is less precisely specified than claimed and cannot be reproduced unambiguously from the equations.

The “end-to-end,” “lightweight,” and “only RGB” framing requires qualification. The complete system includes an external YOLOE-L segmentation model, category-specific calibration, an A*-based expert using privileged maps and GPS during training, and simulator-only ground-truth distance and masks for rewards and auxiliary supervision. RGB-only sensing at inference is valuable, but the full pipeline is neither a single end-to-end model nor fully represented by the stated 130M policy parameter count.

The manuscript initially motivates goals described by free-form language, yet its actual benchmark and method operate on category names; the conclusion itself acknowledges an inability to follow free-form instructions. The broad language-understanding claim is therefore unsupported by the evaluation.

The auxiliary segmentation task may partly learn to reconstruct information already supplied as the current input mask. Although its navigation benefit is empirically demonstrated, the experiments do not establish the proposed explanation that it creates a temporally grounded semantic representation, and the exact supervision target during predicted-mask fine-tuning is insufficiently explicit.

Collision count is a weak safety measure because it is strongly confounded by episode duration and success. The paper recognizes this for the failing PPO baseline but continues to compare raw counts across methods with different success rates and trajectory lengths. Collision rate per step and collision-conditioned success would support the safety claims more convincingly.

Evidence beyond HM3D-OVON remains limited. The real-robot section contains only two qualitative demonstrations, uses a separately trained wide-FOV version, and reports risky behavior near goals; it does not provide enough trials, baselines, or quantitative outcomes to substantiate robust real-world transfer.

Several reproducibility and reporting details are incomplete or inconsistent, including the unavailable code location in the submitted manuscript, the full calibrated threshold list and selection data, detector fine-tuning details, and GPU memory reported as 3486/4992 “GB,” which apparently means MB. These are mostly presentation or reproducibility issues rather than reasons to reject the core empirical contribution.
